checks.title: Bad news held back
checks.question: When the team learns something bad (a slip, a data problem, a design that will not work), how quickly and to whom is it reported, with a next step? Is there anything the team knows today that the sponsor does not?
checks.why: The team knew for six weeks that the source could not deliver hourly data. They hoped to find a workaround and said nothing, so the sponsor learned it from the source owner instead.

evidence.looks_like: Status reports and the issue log that raise problems within days of their discovery, each with an impact and a proposed next step.

signals: Issues appear in the RAID log weeks before they appear in any status report.
Status reports contain only achievements.
Words such as "minor", "under control" or "being looked at" used for issues that later became major.
checks.contradiction: Compare the RAID log dates with status report dates: an issue logged long before it was reported is news that was held back.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the team: "What do we know that we have not told the sponsor?" and report it this week.

checks.title: Technical words used with business people
checks.question: Are documents and reports written for the business in plain words, with technical terms explained or left out? When the business owner signs something, do they understand what it means for them?
checks.why: The design said history would be "type 1 for most dimensions". The business owner signed it, not realising it meant old addresses would be overwritten and last year's regional figures would change.

evidence.looks_like: Business-facing documents that state consequences in business terms ("last year's figures by region will change when a customer moves"), with a short glossary for unavoidable terms.

signals: Status or sign-off documents for the business use unexplained abbreviations and technical terms.
Decisions are described by their technical option, not by their effect on users.
No glossary in documents read by business stakeholders.
checks.contradiction: Compare a decision record with the business owner's own description of it (in notes or e-mail): if they describe a different consequence, the decision was not understood.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner to explain the three biggest decisions back in their own words.

checks.title: Agreed in a meeting, lost afterwards
checks.question: Does every important meeting end with written actions and decisions, sent to the people affected and copied into the decision log or RAID log? A month from now, will anyone remember what was agreed today?
checks.why: The source owner agreed in a meeting to provide a daily extract by a set time. Nothing was written, the owner moved on, and the successor had never heard of it.

evidence.looks_like: Short meeting notes with actions (owner and date) and decisions, sent the same day, and decisions copied into the decision log.

signals: No meeting notes, or notes without actions and owners.
Actions in notes that never appear again in later notes or status reports.
Phrases such as "as discussed" referring to something with no written record.
checks.contradiction: Compare meeting notes with the decision log and RAID log: decisions and actions in the notes that are missing from the logs have been lost.
checks.fail_fast: After the next meeting, send three lines within an hour: decided, actions, open questions.

checks.title: Nobody knows who to call
checks.question: Is there a contact list for the project and the systems it depends on, including who to call when a source changes or a load fails, and how to escalate? If the pipeline fails at night in the first week of production, who is woken up and who do they call?
checks.why: A source was changed without notice and the load failed. Nobody knew who owned the source, so it took three days to find the right person while the reports stayed empty.

evidence.looks_like: A contact and escalation list for the team, each source, the platform, security and operations, with named people and a deputy for each.

signals: No contact or escalation list in the stakeholder map or runbook.
Source systems named in the architecture with no named owner.
Escalation described as "raise with management".
checks.contradiction: Compare the architecture's list of sources and systems with the contact list: a system with no contact is one that will fail silently.
checks.fail_fast: For each source, find the named owner and confirm they will tell the team before changing it.

checks.title: Assumptions never shared with the business
checks.question: Have the assumptions behind the estimate and plan been shown to the sponsor and the business owner, and do they know what changes if one of them breaks? If an assumption fails, will the business be surprised that the plan ever depended on it?
checks.why: The estimate assumed the business would provide testers for two weeks. The business never knew; when no testers came, user acceptance slipped by a month and the team was blamed.

evidence.looks_like: The key assumptions repeated in status reports and sign-off packs, with their current state (holding, at risk, broken).

signals: Status reports and steering packs do not mention assumptions.
Assumptions that require business action (testers, decisions, data) are not assigned to a business person.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate's assumptions with the status reports: assumptions in the estimate that never appear in any report have not been shared.
checks.fail_fast: Add a three-line "assumptions this plan depends on" box to the next status report.

checks.title: No regular rhythm for updates
checks.question: Is there an agreed rhythm for telling stakeholders what was learned, what changed, and what is needed from them? Which stakeholder will say they heard nothing for a month?
checks.why: Updates went out only when there was good news. Stakeholders filled the silence with rumours and the sponsor started asking for daily reports, which took the team's time away from the work.

evidence.looks_like: A communication plan stating who gets what and how often, and status reports that follow it.

signals: No communication plan.
Gaps of several weeks between status reports.
Status reports go to the sponsor only.
checks.contradiction: Compare the communication plan with the actual status reports: a planned weekly update that appears monthly is a rhythm that broke.
checks.fail_fast: Send a three-line update this Friday: what we learned, what changed, what we need from you.

checks.title: The rough guess became the promise
checks.question: Has the estimate been redone since the first rough guess, and does everyone quoting a date or a budget know which version they are quoting? Imagine it is six months from now and the project is late: was the date we are judged against the one somebody guessed before anyone looked at the data?
checks.why: A number given in a corridor before discovery was written into the budget. Discovery found twice the work, but the plan was expected to confirm the guess, so the project was "late" from its first week.

evidence.looks_like: An estimate history showing the rough estimate, the discovery estimate and later re-estimates, each dated, with the baseline that sign-off accepted clearly marked.

signals: The same number appears in the first brief, the discovery document and the plan, unchanged.
The estimate has no date or version, so nobody can tell whether it came before or after discovery.
Status reports measure progress against a figure that is older than the discovery document.
Phrases such as "as agreed at the outset" or "the approved budget" with no link to how it was built.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate with the plan: if the plan's end date or budget matches the stage-2 rough estimate rather than the discovery estimate, the guess has become the promise.
checks.fail_fast: Put the rough estimate and the discovery estimate side by side in front of the sponsor and ask which one the plan is built on.

checks.title: One number instead of a range
checks.question: Is the estimate given as a range, with the reason for its width? If the project overruns, will anyone be able to say whether the overrun was inside the range we said was possible?
checks.why: "Six weeks" was heard as a commitment. "Five to eight weeks if access arrives in week one" would have been a plan, and the slip to seven weeks would have been expected rather than a crisis.

evidence.looks_like: A low and a high figure (or a most-likely figure with a stated spread), and a sentence on what would move it toward either end.

signals: The estimate is a single figure in days, weeks or money with no low and high value.
The width of the range does not narrow from the rough estimate to the discovery estimate.
The range is the same percentage on every item, which suggests it was added, not reasoned.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate with the status reports: a range in the estimate but a single committed date in every status report means the range was dropped on the way to the stakeholders.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the person who wrote the estimate for the worst realistic case. If they can name one without hesitating, it belongs in the document.

checks.title: An estimate with no written assumptions
checks.question: Which assumptions does the estimate depend on, and which one, if wrong, would move it the most? If the estimate turns out wrong, will we be able to point to the assumption that broke?
checks.why: The estimate assumed the source data was clean and that one person would test. Neither was written down, so when both failed, the overrun looked like the team's fault instead of a known risk.

evidence.looks_like: A numbered list of assumptions next to the estimate, the most sensitive ones marked, and each one also logged in the RAID log with an owner.

signals: No "assumptions" heading or list anywhere in or near the estimate.
Assumptions are written as one line, such as "standard assumptions apply".
Assumptions exist in the estimate but none of them appear in the RAID log.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate's assumptions with the RAID log: an assumption in one but not the other is either unmanaged or was never the real basis of the estimate.
checks.fail_fast: Pick the riskiest assumption and test it this week, for example by requesting the access or pulling one real extract.

checks.title: Invisible work left out of the estimate
checks.question: Does the estimate include the work that is not building: getting access, setting up environments, testing, fixing data, rehearsing the cut-over, documentation and handover? If we run out of time, will it be because the build took longer, or because this work was never counted?
checks.why: The build finished on time. Then access approvals, test data, two cut-over rehearsals and the runbook took another five weeks that nobody had planned for.

evidence.looks_like: Separate lines for access and onboarding, environments, testing (including reconciliation and user acceptance), data fixes, history load, cut-over and rollback rehearsal, runbook, handover and hypercare.

signals: The estimate lists only build items (pipelines, tables, reports).
Testing is a fixed percentage added at the end rather than counted per item.
Words such as "cut-over", "handover", "access", "environment" or "hypercare" do not appear in the estimate.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate with the plan: plan tasks for testing, cut-over or handover that have no matching line in the estimate are unfunded work.
checks.fail_fast: Read the estimate against the ten lifecycle stages and ask, for each stage after build, which line pays for it.

checks.title: Guessed, not counted
checks.question: Was the estimate built by counting the things the project will deliver (sources, tables, rules, reports, interfaces) and multiplying by a rate, or was it a total someone felt was right? Could another person rebuild the number from the document?
checks.why: The estimate was "about three months" for the whole project. When it was finally counted there were forty tables and twelve reports, which at the team's real rate was nearer six months.

evidence.looks_like: A table of counted items by type and complexity, a rate per item, where the rate came from, and the total.

signals: The estimate is a total with no breakdown, or a breakdown by phase only.
No counts of sources, tables, rules or reports appear anywhere in the documents.
The rate per item is not stated or not explained.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate with the requirements or data model: if they list more sources, tables or reports than the estimate counted, the estimate is short.
checks.fail_fast: Count the items in the requirements yourself and divide the estimate by the count. If the effort per item looks implausibly small, it probably is.

checks.title: Never corrected against actual progress
checks.question: Is actual effort compared with the estimate at least every two weeks, and has the estimate been changed when the real rate differed? If we finish late, will we have known it two months before or two days before?
checks.why: The thin slice took three times longer than planned per table. Nobody re-estimated, and the gap only showed when the last month of the plan arrived with half the tables still to build.

evidence.looks_like: A re-estimate after the thin slice and then every two weeks, showing items done, the real rate, and the forecast finish, with changes explained.

signals: The estimate document has one version and its date is before build started.
Status reports show percent complete but never a forecast end date or rate.
No mention of a thin slice or of the rate it achieved.
checks.contradiction: Compare status reports with the estimate: if progress reports show fewer items finished than the estimate's rate predicts, but the end date never moves, the estimate is not being corrected.
checks.fail_fast: Divide items finished so far by weeks spent, and project the finish date from that rate today.

checks.title: History load and data fixing underestimated
checks.question: Has the work of loading history and dealing with poor source data been estimated separately, using a profile of the real data? If the history load is what delays go-live, will that surprise anyone?
checks.why: The pipelines worked on a month of data. Ten years of history held old codes, broken keys and a format change, and checking the old numbers with the business took longer than building the pipelines.

evidence.looks_like: Separate estimate lines for the history load (volume, number of runs, reconciliation with the business) and for data fixes, sized from a profile of real data.

signals: The history load is not mentioned in the estimate, or it is one line with a small number.
The estimate says data quality is "assumed acceptable" with no profile behind it.
There is no data profiling section in the discovery document.
checks.contradiction: Compare the discovery profiling results with the estimate: if the profile found quality problems but the estimate has no line for fixing or handling them, the estimate ignored the evidence.
checks.fail_fast: Load one year of real history in a test environment and time it, and count the rows that fail basic rules.

checks.title: Runbook missing or written at the end
checks.question: Is there a runbook that operations have read and used: what runs when, how to tell it failed, how to rerun safely, and who to call? If a load fails on the first night after the team has gone, can operations fix it?
checks.why: The runbook was written in the last week and never tried. On the first failure operations reran the whole load, which doubled a month of figures.

evidence.looks_like: A runbook started in build and finished before deploy, covering schedule, monitoring, alerts, common failures with fixes, safe rerun steps and contacts, used in at least one failure drill.

signals: No runbook or operations guide among the documents.
The runbook is planned only for the last week before go-live.
The runbook has headings but sections marked "to be completed".
checks.contradiction: Compare the runbook with the architecture: jobs, sources or failure points in the architecture that the runbook does not mention will be unsupported.
checks.fail_fast: Break one job in the test environment and ask operations to recover it using only the runbook.

checks.title: Decision log and data dictionary not ready to hand over
checks.question: Will the support team receive a current decision log and data dictionary that explain why things are the way they are? When someone asks "why does this table work like this?" after the team has left, where is the answer?
checks.why: The support team "fixed" a rule that looked wrong. It had been agreed with finance a year before, but the decision was only in an old e-mail thread, and the change broke month-end reporting.

evidence.looks_like: A decision log and a data dictionary that match what is in production, reviewed as part of project closure.

signals: The decision log stops well before the end of build.
The data dictionary does not cover tables or rules added during build.
Handover lists code and access but not decisions or definitions.
checks.contradiction: Compare the data dictionary with the delivered data model or test results: rules in production that are not in the dictionary are unexplained.
checks.fail_fast: Ask someone outside the team to explain one business rule using only the handed-over documents.

checks.title: Knowledge transfer never tested
checks.question: Has the support team made at least one real change and one real recovery while the project team watched? If the project team left tomorrow, could the support team run and change this system?
checks.why: Knowledge transfer was two presentation sessions. The first change request after closure took the support team a month, and the project team had to be called back.

evidence.looks_like: Planned handover sessions with hands-on tasks, and a record of a change and a recovery done by the support team themselves.

signals: Knowledge transfer is a single line or a few presentation sessions in the plan.
The support team is not named, or joins only at the end.
No hands-on tasks are planned for the support team.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan's handover time with the size of the system in the architecture: a short handover for a large system means much will not transfer.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the support team to make one small real change this sprint, with the project team only watching.

checks.title: Support model not agreed
checks.question: Is it agreed who supports the system after go-live, in which hours, how fast they respond, how long the project team stays during the early weeks, and who pays? On the first weekend in production, who answers a failure?
checks.why: The project assumed the central support team would take over; the support team assumed the project would. After go-live a failed weekend load went unnoticed until Monday morning.

evidence.looks_like: A signed support model: support team, hours, response times, escalation, early-life support period, and the criteria for ending it.

signals: No support model, or one that says "business as usual support".
The support team has not been asked to accept the system.
Support hours do not match the freshness promised to users.
checks.contradiction: Compare the support model with the non-functional requirements: data promised by 7 a.m. but support starting at 9 a.m. means nobody fixes a night failure in time.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the support team lead whether they have agreed to take this system, and on what terms.

checks.title: Benefits never measured
checks.question: Is there a plan to measure, after go-live, the benefits promised at the start, against the baseline taken before? A year after closure, can anyone prove the project was worth its cost?
checks.why: The business case promised hours saved each month. Nobody measured hours before or after, so the project could not show any return and the platform's next phase was refused.

evidence.looks_like: A benefits list with baseline values, the date and method of measurement after go-live, and an owner who will report the result.

signals: The business case or goals have no baseline figures.
No benefits review is planned after go-live.
The project closure report does not mention benefits.
checks.contradiction: Compare the goals in the discovery document with the closure or status reports: goals that are never reported on were never measured.
checks.fail_fast: Record today's value of each promised benefit, so there is something to compare against later.

checks.title: No exit criteria for early-life support
checks.question: Are there written criteria for ending the early weeks of close support after go-live (for example a number of clean runs, reconciled loads and no critical defects)? How will we know the system is ready to be left alone, rather than the team simply running out of time?
checks.why: The project team left after two weeks because the budget ended. Month-end processing, which had never run in production, failed the following week with nobody who knew the system.

evidence.looks_like: Written exit criteria for early-life support, covering at least one full business cycle, reconciled production loads and agreed defect levels.

signals: The plan ends at go-live, or has a fixed support period with no criteria.
Period-end or yearly processes are not mentioned in the early-life support period.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan's early-life support period with the business calendar in the requirements: if the period ends before a month-end or other key cycle has run, the riskiest run happens unsupported.
checks.fail_fast: Ask: "Which business cycle has not yet run in production?" and keep support in place until it has.

checks.title: Dates set before the dependencies were known
checks.question: Were the milestones set after the dependencies (access, environments, source changes, other teams, approvals) were listed and confirmed with the people who own them? If the first milestone slips, will it be because of something outside the team that nobody had asked about?
checks.why: The go-live date was announced first. The source team's change freeze, the security review and the network change each added weeks, and none had been asked about when the date was set.

evidence.looks_like: A dependency list with each owner, the date they committed to, and the plan tasks that wait on it.

signals: Milestone dates appear in the brief or charter before any dependency list exists.
The plan has no dependencies, or lists them without owners or dates.
External teams named in the architecture do not appear in the plan.
checks.contradiction: Compare the architecture with the plan: every system or team the architecture relies on should appear as a dependency in the plan; one that does not is an unplanned wait.
checks.fail_fast: Phone the owner of the biggest external dependency and ask for the date they can deliver it, in writing.

checks.title: Risks listed, not managed
checks.question: Does each top risk have an owner, a trigger that tells us it is happening, a mitigation that is being done, and a date it was last reviewed? Looking back after a failure, will the cause be on the risk log with nothing done about it?
checks.why: "Source data quality may be poor" sat on the risk log for six months with no owner. It was exactly the reason the project missed its date.

evidence.looks_like: A short top-risks list where each risk has an owner, a trigger, a mitigation with a due date, and a recent review date.

signals: Risks with no owner, or with a team rather than a person as owner.
No triggers or mitigation actions, only descriptions.
The risk log has not changed in several weeks while status reports describe new problems.
checks.contradiction: Compare the RAID log with status reports: problems in the status reports that were never on the risk log, or risks that became issues without the log changing, mean the log is not used.
checks.fail_fast: Take the top three risks and ask each owner what they did about it this week.

checks.title: Decisions not written down
checks.question: Is there a decision log recording the options, the choice, the reason, who decided and when? When a decision is reopened by someone who was not in the room, what will we show them?
checks.why: The team agreed to keep only the latest customer address. Three months later a new manager asked why history was missing, and with no record the decision was reversed and the work redone.

evidence.looks_like: A decision log or short decision records: context, options, decision, reason, owner, who signed, date.

signals: No decision log or decision records exist among the project documents.
Meeting notes contain "agreed" or "decided" but no decision log entry matches.
Architecture choices are stated with no record of the options considered.
checks.contradiction: Compare meeting notes or status reports with the decision log: a decision mentioned in notes but not in the log is one that can be lost.
checks.fail_fast: List the last five important choices from memory and check how many are in the log.

checks.title: Green until it is red
checks.question: Do status reports show amber or red when something is slipping, with the reason and the next step? If the project fails suddenly, will the reports from the month before have shown it as green?
checks.why: Status stayed green for four months while the team quietly fell behind. It went red two weeks before go-live, when there was nothing left to do but move the date.

evidence.looks_like: Status reports where the colour is based on stated rules (for example forecast versus baseline), and where amber appears early with a recovery action.

signals: Every status report is green.
The status colour does not change while the forecast date or open issues change.
No forecast finish date, only activities done.
checks.contradiction: Compare status reports with the RAID log and the estimate: a green status alongside rising issues, a rate below the estimate, or slipping dependencies means the colour is not telling the truth.
checks.fail_fast: Write down the rule for red, amber and green today and apply it to the last report.

checks.title: Testing and deployment left to the end
checks.question: Does the plan have testing and deployment to a production-like environment starting in the first weeks of build, rather than after it? If go-live slips, will it be because the first real deployment happened a month before the date?
checks.why: Everything was built, then tested, then deployed. The first deployment found network, permission and performance problems that took longer to fix than the build had taken.

evidence.looks_like: A test strategy and a release approach agreed in discovery, a first deployment of a thin slice in the first weeks, and "done" defined as tested and deployed.

signals: No test strategy or deployment document exists, or it says "to be defined".
The plan has testing and deployment as single phases after build.
The definition of done mentions coding but not testing or deployment.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan with the test strategy: if the strategy describes continuous testing but the plan has one test phase at the end, the plan wins and testing will be squeezed.
checks.fail_fast: Deploy the thin slice to the test environment this week, through the real release route.

checks.title: Key-person risk
checks.question: Is there any part of the project that only one person understands or can do, and are the people the plan needs named and available when it needs them? If one person leaves next month, what stops?
checks.why: One developer understood the source system. When they moved to another project mid-build, the team lost six weeks rediscovering what they knew.

evidence.looks_like: Named people for each role with their availability, a second person for every critical area, and key-person risks on the RAID log.

signals: The same person's name appears as owner for most technical items.
Roles are listed as "to be hired" or "to be confirmed" for work in the next stage.
No mention of availability, leave or shared allocation.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan with the stakeholder map or team list: a plan that needs a role the team list does not have, or a person allocated part-time who carries full-time tasks, will slip.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each team member which area they could not cover if a colleague were away for a month.

checks.title: The plan ignores the estimate's assumptions
checks.question: Does the plan use the same assumptions as the estimate (start of access, team size, environment availability, source readiness)? When the plan slips, will it be because it assumed something the estimate never did?
checks.why: The estimate assumed access in week three; the plan assumed week one. Nobody compared them, and the plan was two weeks behind before work started.

evidence.looks_like: A plan that lists the estimate's key assumptions and shows where each one sits on the timeline.

signals: The plan does not mention the estimate or its assumptions.
The plan's team size or start dates differ from the estimate's.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate's assumptions with the plan's dates and staffing: any mismatch is a slip already built in.
checks.fail_fast: Put the estimate's assumptions next to the first four weeks of the plan and look for disagreements.

checks.title: Open decisions with no owner, deadline or default
checks.question: Does every open decision have an owner, a date by which it is needed, and a default that applies if nobody decides? If the team is blocked next month, will it be waiting on a decision nobody owns?
checks.why: The choice between daily and hourly loads stayed open for ten weeks because nobody owned it. The team built for both, and later threw half away.

evidence.looks_like: An open-decisions list with the question, options, owner, the date needed, the default and the effect of deciding late.

signals: Open questions listed with no owner or due date.
Items the build depends on are marked "TBD" or "to be confirmed".
The same open question appears in several consecutive status reports.
checks.contradiction: Compare the open decisions with the plan: a task scheduled to start before the decision it depends on is due will either stall or be redone.
checks.fail_fast: Give every open decision an owner and a default today, and tell the owners the default applies on the due date.

checks.title: Discovery with no timebox
checks.question: Does discovery have a fixed length, a cost, and a list of exit criteria? If discovery runs for months or is squeezed into days, which risks will we carry into the build without having tested them?
checks.why: Discovery was squeezed into three days to "start building faster". The riskiest beliefs were never tested, and they surfaced one by one during the build.

evidence.looks_like: A discovery plan of a few weeks with weekly goals, its own estimate, named reviewers and written exit criteria.

signals: No discovery stage in the plan, or no end date for it.
Discovery has no estimate of its own.
No exit criteria for discovery sign-off.
checks.contradiction: Compare the discovery exit criteria with the discovery document: criteria that are not met but sign-off still happened show the timebox beat the evidence.
checks.fail_fast: Write the discovery exit criteria now and agree the end date with the sponsor.

checks.title: Access and environments treated as admin
checks.question: Were access to sources, environments and tools requested in the first week and tracked as dependencies with owners and dates? If the build starts late, will it be because the team waited weeks for access?
checks.why: Access requests were raised when build started. Approvals took six weeks, so the team spent the first sprints on paper designs that the real data later contradicted.

evidence.looks_like: A list of every access and environment request with the date raised, the approver, the expected date and its current state.

signals: No access or environment requests are listed in the plan or RAID log.
Access is described as "assumed" or "will be arranged".
Discovery has no real data extract because access had not arrived.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan's start of build with the access request dates: a build that starts before access is expected is planned to wait.
checks.fail_fast: Raise every access request today and record the date each one arrives.

checks.title: Vague words in the requirements
checks.question: Has every vague word in the requirements, such as "real-time", "fast", "all data", "user-friendly", "accurate" or "complete", been replaced with a number or a test? If the users reject the system at the end, will it be because we each read those words differently?
checks.why: "Real-time" meant within a second to the sponsor and by the next morning to the team. The design was built for daily loads and had to be rebuilt late in the project.

evidence.looks_like: Every quality word paired with a measure, for example "available by 7 a.m. on working days" instead of "timely", or "the last three years" instead of "all history".

signals: Words such as real-time, near real-time, fast, quickly, timely, all data, complete, accurate, user-friendly, intuitive, seamless, scalable or robust appear without a number next to them.
Lists of required data or reports end with "etc." or "and so on".
checks.contradiction: Compare the requirements with the architecture: if the requirement says "real-time" and the architecture schedules a daily batch, someone's reading of the word is wrong.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the requester to put a number on each vague word in a fifteen-minute call, and write the answers down.

checks.title: No acceptance criteria
checks.question: Does every requirement have acceptance criteria that the data can be tested against? At user acceptance, how will we and the business agree that a requirement is met?
checks.why: Requirements said "show monthly sales by region". At user acceptance the business compared it with their own report, got a different number, and nobody had agreed in advance which one was right.

evidence.looks_like: For each requirement, one or more criteria in the form "given this data, the result is this", ideally with a known figure the business already trusts.

signals: Requirements or user stories have no "acceptance criteria" or "done when" section.
Acceptance criteria repeat the requirement in other words rather than describing a test.
Backlog items are marked ready for build without criteria.
checks.contradiction: Compare the requirements with the test strategy: requirements that have no matching test, or tests that trace to no requirement, show the two were written apart.
checks.fail_fast: Take the three most important requirements and write a test for each with the business owner, using a figure from a report they already trust.

checks.title: Business definitions not agreed and signed
checks.question: Are the key business definitions (for example revenue, active customer, order date) written down and signed by the person who owns each one? If two departments see different numbers after go-live, which signed definition settles it?
checks.why: Sales counted revenue when the order was booked; finance counted it when it was paid. Both signed the requirements, which said "revenue", and the dashboard was disowned by one of them in the first week.

evidence.looks_like: A definitions list with the exact rule for each term, the grain, the owner who signed it and the date.

signals: The data dictionary has names but no rules, owners or sign-off.
The same term is used in requirements from different departments with no definition.
Definitions are marked "to be confirmed" in a document that has passed discovery sign-off.
checks.contradiction: Compare the requirements with the data model: if a term in the requirements has a different rule, or no rule, in the data model, the definition was never agreed.
checks.fail_fast: Ask two of the main consumers to write their own definition of the top five terms separately, then compare the answers.

checks.title: Requirements written without looking at the data
checks.question: Were the requirements checked against a profile of the real source data? If a requirement turns out to be impossible, will we find out in discovery or in testing?
checks.why: The requirement asked for sales by product category. The source had no category for a third of products, which only came to light when the report was tested.

evidence.looks_like: A data profile per source (volumes, keys, nulls, odd values) and a note against each requirement saying which source fields support it and any gaps found.

signals: No data profiling section or results in the discovery document.
Requirements name fields or attributes that do not appear in any source description.
Phrases such as "data to be confirmed" or "assumed available" against required fields.
checks.contradiction: Compare the requirements with the data model or source mapping: a required field with no source mapped to it is a requirement nobody checked against the data.
checks.fail_fast: Pull one real extract from each source and map the top ten requirements to actual columns in an afternoon.

checks.title: The users are not the requesters
checks.question: Have the people who will use the output every day been asked what they need, or only the people who requested it? If nobody uses the system three months after go-live, will it be because it answered the requester's question and not the users'?
checks.why: A director requested a dashboard and approved the design. The analysts who were meant to use it needed row-level detail to act on, kept their old reports, and the dashboard went unused.

evidence.looks_like: Named users or user groups, how they will use the output, which decisions it supports, and evidence that some of them took part in workshops and will take part in user acceptance testing.

signals: Requirements name only a sponsor or requester, not users.
No user workshops, interviews or user personas are mentioned.
User acceptance testers are not named, or are the same person as the requester.
checks.contradiction: Compare the stakeholder map with the requirements sources: user groups on the map who are not listed as contributors to the requirements were never asked.
checks.fail_fast: Show a rough mock-up or a real sample of the output to three actual users and ask what decision they would make with it.

checks.title: Non-functional needs missing
checks.question: Are freshness, volume and growth, recovery time and acceptable data loss, retention, and who may see what written as requirements with numbers? If the system works but is rejected, will it be because it is too slow, too stale, or unrecoverable?
checks.why: Nobody asked how fresh the data had to be or how quickly it had to recover. After the first overnight failure the business found out it would take a day to recover, and the system was not accepted.

evidence.looks_like: A short non-functional list: freshness deadline, expected volume and growth, how long it may be down, how much data may be lost, how long data is kept, and access rules.

signals: No "non-functional" heading in the requirements.
Freshness, recovery or retention are mentioned only as "to be agreed".
Volume is described in words ("large") rather than numbers.
checks.contradiction: Compare the requirements with the runbook or support model: if the runbook promises recovery within hours but no requirement says what is needed, or the reverse, the two disagree on what was promised.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner: "If this is down for a day, what happens?" and write down the answer as a number.

checks.title: Goals with no measure of success
checks.question: What business result is this project for, how will it be measured, and what is the measure today? A year after go-live, how will anyone know whether it was worth it?
checks.why: The goal was "better insight into customers". No measure was agreed, so at closure the project could not show any benefit, and the next request for funding was refused.

evidence.looks_like: Two or three goals, each with a measure, today's value (the baseline), a target, and where the data for measuring it will come from.

signals: Goals are written as activities ("build a data platform") rather than results.
No baseline figures are given for any goal.
Success measures need data the project does not collect.
checks.contradiction: Compare the goals in the discovery document with the scope: a goal whose measure depends on data or reports that are out of scope cannot be measured.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the sponsor to state the one number they hope will change, and check today whether that number can be produced.

checks.title: Scope written only as "in"
checks.question: Is there a written list of what is out of scope, as well as what is in? When someone says "I assumed that was included", which document will we point to?
checks.why: The scope listed the tables to build. The business assumed the reports on top were included too, and the argument cost a month and the sponsor's trust.

evidence.looks_like: Three lists, in scope, out of scope and later, each item specific enough that a stranger could say which list a new request belongs to.

signals: No "out of scope" heading or list in the discovery, scope or requirements document.
The out-of-scope list is generic ("anything not listed above").
checks.contradiction: Compare the scope with the requirements: a requirement that is neither in the in-scope list nor explicitly out is a future argument.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner to read only the out-of-scope list and say which item surprises them.

checks.title: The data scope traps left silent
checks.question: Has each of the ten data scope traps been written down as in, out or later: history and backfill, deletes at the source, late and corrected data, changes over time, bad rows, source data quality, personal data, reports and dashboards, access and onboarding, and recovery? Which of them will someone assume was included?
checks.why: Nobody wrote down whether deleted customers should disappear from the reports. The business assumed yes, the team assumed no, and the gap was found by an auditor.

evidence.looks_like: A table with one row per trap, the decision (in, out or later), who decided and why.

signals: Several of the words history, backfill, delete, late, correction, bad rows, quality, personal data, reports, access and recovery do not appear in the scope section.
Traps are mentioned but marked "to be confirmed" after discovery sign-off.
checks.contradiction: Compare the scope with the architecture: a trap the architecture handles (for example history kept) that the scope does not mention, or the reverse, shows the two were never reconciled.
checks.fail_fast: Walk the ten traps with the business owner in thirty minutes and record each answer.

checks.title: Scope creep with no change process
checks.question: Is there an agreed way to handle a new request: who can raise it, how it is sized, who decides, and how the plan and estimate change? If the project ends late, how much of the lateness will be work that was added without anyone deciding to add it?
checks.why: Each request was small and agreed in a meeting. After three months, a fifth of the work had never been estimated, the date had not moved, and the team was blamed for the slip.

evidence.looks_like: A written change process and a change log where each change shows the request, its size, its effect on date and cost, the decision and who made it.

signals: No "change control", "change request" or "change process" in the plan.
Status reports mention new items that do not appear in the original scope or in any change log.
Meeting notes include "can we also add" with no follow-up decision.
checks.contradiction: Compare the latest status report or backlog with the signed scope: items in the backlog that are not in the scope and have no change record are unmanaged creep.
checks.fail_fast: Count backlog items added since sign-off and check how many have a recorded decision.

checks.title: "Phase 2" used as a hiding place
checks.question: Is everything labelled "phase 2" or "later" actually planned, funded and owned, and does the business know that phase 2 may never happen? If phase 2 is cancelled, will the first phase still be useful on its own?
checks.why: Hard items such as history and data quality were moved to phase 2 to make the first phase look affordable. Phase 2 was never funded, and phase 1 was unusable without them.

evidence.looks_like: A "later" list in which each item states whether phase 1 depends on it, an owner, and whether funding exists, plus a statement that phase 1 is usable without them.

signals: Many items marked "phase 2", "future phase" or "later" with no dates or owners.
Phase 2 has no estimate or budget.
Items that the main goal depends on are listed under phase 2.
checks.contradiction: Compare the goals or success measures with the phase-2 list: a goal that can only be met by phase-2 items means phase 1 alone does not deliver the value promised.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the sponsor: "If there is no phase 2, would you still pay for phase 1 as written?"

checks.title: MVP 1 is too big
checks.question: Is the first MVP the smallest slice that gives real value and proves the hardest parts work end to end? If the first release slips by months, will it be because it tried to do everything at once?
checks.why: MVP 1 contained eight sources and every report. Nothing reached production for nine months, so no real feedback arrived until it was too late to change direction.

evidence.looks_like: An MVP 1 that can reach production within a few months, chosen for value and for testing the riskiest beliefs, with later MVPs listed in order of dependency and value.

signals: MVP 1 contains most or all of the in-scope items.
The first production release date is more than about three months after build starts.
The reason for the MVP order is not written down.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan's MVP 1 with the estimate: if MVP 1 holds most of the estimated effort, it is the whole project with a different label.
checks.fail_fast: Ask what could be removed from MVP 1 while it still gives one group of users a real answer.

checks.title: Scope not signed by the business owner
checks.question: Has the person who will judge success signed the in, out and later lists, and is that signature recorded with a date? If scope is disputed later, whose signature ends the argument?
checks.why: The scope was agreed with a delegate. The real business owner saw it for the first time at user acceptance and rejected half of the out-of-scope list.

evidence.looks_like: A dated sign-off record naming the business owner, the version of the scope signed, and any conditions.

signals: The scope document has no approver, approval date or version.
Approval is recorded as "agreed in meeting" without a name.
The approver is not the business owner named in the stakeholder map.
checks.contradiction: Compare the scope sign-off with the stakeholder map: if the person who signed is not the one the map names as the decision owner, the sign-off may not hold.
checks.fail_fast: Send the out-of-scope list to the business owner today and ask for a written yes.

checks.title: Only the sponsor is managed
checks.question: Does the stakeholder map include the people outside the weekly meeting who can block go-live: source system owners, operations, security, the platform team and downstream users? Who could stop this project in its last month that we have not spoken to in its first?
checks.why: The sponsor was kept happy every week. Security saw the design for the first time two weeks before go-live, required personal data to be masked, and the release slipped by two months.

evidence.looks_like: A stakeholder map naming each person or group, what they care about, what they can approve or block, when they were last spoken to, and how they are kept informed.

signals: No stakeholder map or communication plan exists.
The map lists only the sponsor, the business owner and the project team.
Operations, security, source owners or downstream consumers are not named anywhere.
checks.contradiction: Compare the architecture with the stakeholder map: every source, platform and consumer in the architecture has an owner who should appear on the map; one who does not is an unmanaged blocker.
checks.fail_fast: List everyone who must say yes before go-live and book a thirty-minute meeting with each one you have not met.

checks.title: Nobody clearly owns the decisions
checks.question: For each kind of decision (scope, definitions, priorities, go-live), is one named person the decision owner? When two senior people disagree, who decides, and how long will we wait?
checks.why: Two directors each believed they owned the project. Every decision was taken twice, the team built to whichever spoke last, and both rejected the result.

evidence.looks_like: A responsibility table (who decides, who is consulted, who is informed) for the main decision types, with one decider per type and a route for escalation.

signals: No responsibility table, or several people marked as the decider for the same thing.
Decision log entries with no named decider.
Phrases such as "the business will decide" without a name.
checks.contradiction: Compare the stakeholder map with the decision log: decisions signed by someone the map does not name as the decider are likely to be reopened.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the sponsor to name, in writing, the one person who decides on scope and definitions.

checks.title: No real numbers shown to the business
checks.question: Have the business users seen real numbers from real data, regularly, before user acceptance testing? If they say "these numbers are wrong" at the end, will it be the first time they have looked?
checks.why: Demos used made-up data that looked fine. The first time the business saw real numbers was user acceptance, and they did not recognise them.

evidence.looks_like: Regular demos, roughly every two weeks, with real data, and a record of what the business said and what changed as a result.

signals: No demos are planned or recorded before the test stage.
Demos are described as using sample, dummy or mock data.
The data profile was not shown to the business owner during discovery.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan with the meeting notes or status reports: planned demos that do not appear in the notes did not happen.
checks.fail_fast: Show the business owner one real number from the thin slice and ask whether they recognise it.

checks.title: Conflicts left unsaid
checks.question: Where stakeholders want different things (speed against cost, one department's definition against another's), is the conflict written down with options and taken to the decision owner? Which disagreement are we avoiding that will surface at sign-off?
checks.why: Finance wanted monthly figures to match the ledger; sales wanted daily figures fast. Nobody named the conflict, the design pleased neither, and both refused to sign.

evidence.looks_like: Conflicts recorded as issues or open decisions, with each side's need, options, a recommendation and a deadline.

signals: Requirements from different groups that contradict each other with no note of the conflict.
Meeting notes saying a topic was "taken offline" repeatedly.
No issues or open decisions involve more than one stakeholder group.
checks.contradiction: Compare requirements from two different stakeholder groups: requirements that cannot both be met, with no decision recorded, are a hidden conflict.
checks.fail_fast: Put the two conflicting needs on one page with options and send it to the decision owner this week.

checks.title: Sign-off without reading
checks.question: Did the people signing get the document in time to read it, and are their findings answered in writing? Is anyone signing something they have not read or do not agree with?
checks.why: Reviewers saw the discovery document for the first time in the sign-off meeting and approved it to keep things moving. Their real objections arrived in the build, where they cost ten times more.

evidence.looks_like: The document sent to reviewers several days before sign-off, a list of findings with written answers, and a sign-off record naming who approved what.

signals: No review comments or findings are recorded before sign-off.
The document was distributed on the same day as the sign-off meeting.
Sign-off is recorded for a group ("the steering committee") with no individual names.
checks.contradiction: Compare the sign-off record with later status reports or change requests: early objections to items that were signed suggest the signers had not read them.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each signer, before the meeting, for their single biggest concern in writing.

checks.title: Success not defined for each stakeholder
checks.question: Has each key stakeholder been asked what success looks like for them and what has gone wrong for them before? If a stakeholder calls the project a failure, will we know in advance what they were measuring?
checks.why: The sponsor wanted lower cost, operations wanted fewer night calls, and users wanted faster reports. The project delivered only faster reports and was seen as a failure by two out of three.

evidence.looks_like: For each key stakeholder, one line on what success means to them and a note of past problems they raised.

signals: The stakeholder map lists names and roles but not interests or success measures.
No record of initial interviews with stakeholders outside the business owner.
checks.contradiction: Compare each stakeholder's success measure with the scope: a measure that nothing in scope can move is a disappointment already planned.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each stakeholder one question this week: "What would make you say this project worked?"

checks.title: Running cost estimated from a real run
checks.question: What will the solution cost to run each month (compute, storage, transfer, licences), and is the figure based on a measured run rather than a guess?
checks.why: The business case assumed a few hundred a month; the first production bill was eleven thousand because the streaming jobs ran around the clock, and the project was paused for review.

evidence.looks_like: A monthly running cost estimate broken down by job and storage, derived from the thin slice or a test run scaled to production volume, agreed with the budget owner.

signals: Cost appears only as build effort, with no running cost.
checks.fail_fast: Read the actual cost of the thin slice's runs and multiply by production volume and schedule.

checks.title: Platform cost guardrails
checks.question: What stops a single team, job or user from running up an unexpected bill (budgets, alerts, limits on compute size, automatic shutdown)?
checks.why: A developer left a large compute cluster running over a holiday weekend, and the month's budget was gone by the fourth.

evidence.looks_like: Budgets with alerts per team or project, policies that cap compute size and enforce automatic shutdown, and a named person who receives cost alerts.

checks.fail_fast: Try to create the largest compute allowed as an ordinary developer in the development environment; the policy should stop you.

checks.title: Cost can be traced to a team and a job
checks.question: Can the running cost be broken down by project, team, environment and job (by tags or separate accounts), so overruns can be traced?
checks.why: The platform bill doubled in one month and nobody could say which project caused it, so every team was asked to cut costs instead of the one that needed to.

evidence.looks_like: A mandatory tagging standard (project, owner, environment), enforced on compute and storage, and a cost report by tag.

checks.fail_fast: Pull last week's cost broken down by project tag; check how much is untagged.

checks.title: No compute running when nothing needs it
checks.question: Is compute sized from real runs and does it stop when idle, rather than staying on or oversized "to be safe"?
checks.why: A job that needed ten minutes of compute held a large cluster for two hours each run because it waited on an upstream file, and nobody noticed for six months.

evidence.looks_like: Compute sizes justified by measured runs, automatic stop or job-scoped compute, waits on upstream data done outside paid compute, and a periodic review of utilisation.

checks.fail_fast: For the three most expensive jobs, compare the time compute was running against the time it was busy.

checks.title: Data quality rules written with owners
checks.question: Which data quality rules apply to each important table, who owns each rule, and are they written down as checks that run on every load?
checks.why: Everyone assumed someone else checked that order totals were positive; a source bug sent negative totals for a week and nobody's check caught it.

evidence.looks_like: A rule list per table (not null, unique, valid values, ranges, referential integrity, business rules), each with a business owner and a severity, implemented as automated checks.

signals: The documents say "data quality checks will be applied" with no list of rules.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner for the five things that would make them distrust the main report, and write each as a rule that runs on today's data.

checks.title: What happens to a row that fails a rule
checks.question: When a row fails a rule, is the batch rejected, the row quarantined, or the row loaded and flagged, and who is told and fixes it?
checks.why: Bad rows were filtered out silently; three thousand orders a day disappeared into a table no one looked at, and sales were understated for a quarter.

evidence.looks_like: An action per rule severity, a quarantine table with reasons, a count of quarantined rows reported to an owner, and a way to reprocess rows once fixed.

checks.fail_fast: Feed a sample with known bad rows in test and check each lands where the design says, with a reason, and that an owner is notified.

checks.title: One poison record does not stop the whole load
checks.question: Can a single malformed record (broken encoding, unparseable value, oversized field) stop the whole pipeline, and how is it isolated?
checks.why: One record with a malformed date crashed the stream parser on every retry; the pipeline was stuck for six hours while all later data waited behind it.

evidence.looks_like: Parsing that captures unreadable records into a side table with the raw content and the error, and a test with deliberately malformed input.

checks.fail_fast: Put one malformed record in the middle of a test input; the rest must load and the bad record must be kept somewhere readable.

checks.title: A source goes quiet or sends far too little
checks.question: Does anything detect a source that sends no data, an empty file, or a much smaller or larger volume than usual?
checks.why: The source sent an empty file after a failed export; the load succeeded, every job was green, and the business saw a day with zero sales before any engineer did.

evidence.looks_like: Freshness and volume checks per source with expected ranges, which fail or alert rather than load quietly.

signals: Monitoring is described only as "job failure alerts".
checks.fail_fast: Run a load with an empty input in test; it must not complete as a green success without someone being told.

checks.title: Real data profiled before design
checks.question: Has real data from every source been profiled (nulls, duplicates, broken keys, odd values, volumes), and was the profile shown to the business owner?
checks.why: The design assumed every order had a customer; profiling in build week three found twenty percent did not, and the model and estimate both had to be redone.

evidence.looks_like: A profile per source table from a real extract (not a sample built by hand), with findings and what was decided about each.

signals: Discovery describes sources from documentation only, with no profiling results.
checks.fail_fast: Pull a real extract of the biggest source table this week and count nulls, duplicates and orphan keys in the columns the design relies on.

checks.title: Detecting hard deletes at the source
checks.question: When a record is physically deleted in the source, how does the platform find out?
checks.why: Cancelled orders were deleted in the source, but the incremental extract only picked up new and changed rows, so the cancelled orders stayed in the warehouse and inflated sales.

evidence.looks_like: For each source, whether deletes happen and how they are captured: change capture with delete events, a periodic full key comparison, or a delete feed from the source.

signals: Incremental loads use a modified-date filter and deletes are not mentioned.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the source owner whether rows are ever deleted, then delete a test row in a source test system and run the load; the platform must reflect it.

checks.title: What a delete means downstream
checks.question: When a source deletes or soft-deletes a record, must it disappear, be flagged, or stay in each layer and report, and who decided?
checks.why: Engineers removed deleted customers from every table, but finance needed them kept for historic invoices, and last year's revenue dropped after a routine load.

evidence.looks_like: A rule per entity (remove, flag with a deleted date, or keep) agreed with the data owner, and how flagged rows are filtered in reports.

checks.fail_fast: Write the delete rule for the top three entities and get the data owner to sign them in one meeting.

checks.title: Deletes flow through derived tables
checks.question: When a source row is deleted, are the aggregates, summaries and extracts built from it recalculated too?
checks.why: The detail table dropped a deleted order, but the daily summary built from it was only ever appended to, so detail and summary disagreed and users stopped trusting both.

evidence.looks_like: Derived tables rebuilt for the affected periods when deletes arrive, and a test that checks detail and summary still agree after a delete.

checks.fail_fast: Delete one source row in test, run the full chain, and compare the summary total against the sum of the detail.

checks.title: A thin slice proved the design end to end
checks.question: Has one source table been pushed through every layer to one report or query in a production-like environment, before the design was signed off?
checks.why: A clean architecture diagram was signed off without ever running; in MVP 1 the team found the source format, network and permissions all differed from the assumptions.

evidence.looks_like: A description of the thin slice, where it ran, what it proved, what it found, and how the design changed as a result.

signals: The architecture shows only target-state diagrams with no evidence of anything having run.
checks.fail_fast: Choose the riskiest source and the most important report, and connect them with the simplest possible pipeline this week.

checks.title: Non-functional needs written as numbers
checks.question: Are the non-functional needs (freshness, volume, recovery, availability, retention, concurrency) written as measurable numbers and agreed with the business?
checks.why: "Near real time" meant five seconds to the business and an hour to the engineers; the gap was found at user acceptance and the design had to be rebuilt.

evidence.looks_like: A table of non-functional needs, each with a number, a measurement method and who agreed it.

signals: Words like "fast", "near real time", "scalable" or "highly available" with no numbers.
checks.fail_fast: Rewrite each non-functional sentence as a number and ask the business owner to confirm it.

checks.title: Grain and keys of every table
checks.question: Is the grain (what one row means) and the key of every target table written down and agreed?
checks.why: The orders table mixed order headers and order lines; summing it double-counted shipping, and two teams built different fixes.

evidence.looks_like: For each table: one sentence for the grain, the key columns, and a uniqueness test on that key.

checks.fail_fast: For each target table, finish the sentence "one row is one …" and test the key for uniqueness.

checks.title: Shared frameworks instead of one-off code
checks.question: Does the platform provide shared, configuration-driven patterns for common work (ingestion, quality checks, logging, history handling), so each pipeline is not hand-built?
checks.why: Forty pipelines were each written differently; a fix to the deduplication logic had to be made forty times, and twelve were missed.

evidence.looks_like: A small set of shared patterns or frameworks with documented configuration, proved by the first two projects, and a decision on what is built versus reused.

checks.fail_fast: Onboard a second source table with the framework and count how many lines of new code it took.

checks.title: Batch or streaming chosen for a reason
checks.question: Is the choice between batch, micro-batch and streaming justified by a stated freshness need and its cost, not by preference?
checks.why: The team built continuous streaming for a report read once a day; it cost eight times a nightly batch and was harder to support.

evidence.looks_like: A decision record linking the processing mode to a freshness number and a running cost comparison.

checks.fail_fast: Ask the consumer what decision they would take differently with data one minute old versus one hour old.

checks.title: Same batch or file arriving twice
checks.question: How is a file, batch or extract that arrives a second time prevented from doubling the numbers?
checks.why: After an outage the source resent yesterday's file, the pipeline loaded it again as new, and revenue on the dashboard doubled for a day before anyone noticed.

evidence.looks_like: A business key or file fingerprint, a record of what has already been loaded, and a test that loads the same input twice.

signals: The architecture describes loads as appends with no key, fingerprint or load register.
The test strategy has no test that resends an input.
checks.fail_fast: Load the same file twice in a test environment; row counts and key totals in every layer must not change after the second load.

checks.title: Rerunning a job changes the result
checks.question: If a job is run again for the same period, does it produce exactly the same result (is every step idempotent)?
checks.why: Operations reran a failed nightly job, but its first half had already appended rows, so the fact table held two copies of the night's orders until month-end reconciliation found them.

evidence.looks_like: Each write described as merge on a key, or replace of a whole partition or period, never a blind append; a rerun test per pipeline; the runbook says reruns are safe.

signals: Writes are described as "insert" or "append" with no key or partition overwrite.
The runbook warns operators not to rerun, or says to clean up by hand before rerunning.
checks.fail_fast: Run the pipeline twice in a row for the same day in test and compare a fingerprint of every output table (counts, sums of key measures); they must be identical.

checks.title: Duplicates already inside the source
checks.question: Does each source have a reliable unique key, and what is the rule when the source itself sends two rows for the same thing?
checks.why: The source table had no primary key and sent the same customer twice with different spellings; joins to it multiplied order rows and inflated sales by eight percent.

evidence.looks_like: A profile showing key uniqueness per source table, the chosen business key, and an agreed rule for duplicates (keep latest, keep all, reject), signed by the data owner.

signals: The data model lists tables without a key, or says "key to be confirmed".
No profiling results for key uniqueness are recorded.
checks.fail_fast: Count rows per proposed key in a real extract of every source table; any key with more than one row needs a written rule before design continues.

checks.title: Replayed events in a stream
checks.question: When the stream redelivers events after a restart or failure (at-least-once delivery), how does the target avoid counting them twice?
checks.why: A consumer restarted from an older position and replayed two hours of events; the counts sink appended them again and the real-time dashboard overstated traffic for the day.

evidence.looks_like: An event id or key plus sequence used to deduplicate, a stated delivery guarantee end to end, and an idempotent or transactional write to the sink.

signals: The design assumes "exactly once" without saying which component provides it.
checks.fail_fast: In test, stop the stream mid-flow, rewind its position by a known number of events, restart, and confirm output counts match the input exactly.

checks.title: Separate environments with separate data
checks.question: Are there separate development, test and production environments, isolated so work in one cannot read or overwrite another's data?
checks.why: A developer ran a cleanup script pointed at what they thought was development; the paths were shared and production tables were wiped the night before a board meeting.

evidence.looks_like: Named environments with separate storage, catalogs or schemas, identities and compute, and a rule that non-production identities cannot write to production.

signals: The platform document describes one workspace or one storage location for all stages.
checks.fail_fast: Using a development identity, try to write to a production table; it must be refused.

checks.title: Access through groups and service identities
checks.question: Is access granted to groups by role with least privilege, and do scheduled jobs run as service identities rather than as a person?
checks.why: Production jobs ran under the lead developer's own account; when she left the company her account was disabled and every nightly job failed.

evidence.looks_like: A role-to-group access model, service identities for jobs in each environment, no direct user grants in production, and who approves access requests.

checks.fail_fast: List who owns and runs each production job; any job owned or run by a named person is a gap.

checks.title: Network path to every source proven early
checks.question: Has a connection from the platform to every source and target been made in a real environment, through firewalls, private links and credentials?
checks.why: The source sat in a data centre behind a firewall; the network change took nine weeks of tickets and MVP 1 waited for it with the team idle.

evidence.looks_like: Each source and target with its connection method, the network changes required, their lead time, and evidence a test connection succeeded.

signals: Connectivity appears as an assumption in the risk log with no date.
checks.fail_fast: Raise the network and credential requests in week one of discovery and pull one row from every source.

checks.title: Platform standards that projects follow
checks.question: Are naming, layer, folder and table standards written down for the platform so every project builds the same way?
checks.why: Three projects named and layered their tables differently; consumers could not tell raw from cleaned data, and a shared lineage view became impossible.

evidence.looks_like: A short standards document covering naming, layers, table types, ownership tags and code structure, with examples, applied by the first project.

checks.fail_fast: Ask two developers to name the same new table independently; if the names differ, the standard is missing or unclear.

checks.title: Project fits the existing platform's standards
checks.question: Does the project follow the existing platform's environments, standards and shared frameworks, and are any exceptions agreed with the platform team?
checks.why: The project built its own ingestion code and its own environment layout; the platform team refused to support it at go-live and it had to be rebuilt.

evidence.looks_like: References to the platform standards and frameworks used, and a decision record for each deviation, signed by the platform team.

checks.fail_fast: Walk the platform team through the architecture for thirty minutes and list every point where they say "we don't do it that way".

checks.title: History load scope and approach
checks.question: How much history will be loaded, from where, and by what approach (one go, in phases, or from archive), and who checks the old numbers?
checks.why: The plan assumed history would come from the same feed as daily loads, but the source only kept ninety days; five years had to come from an archive in another format, adding six weeks.

evidence.looks_like: The number of years in scope, where each year comes from, the load approach and order, the expected volume, and who signs off that historical numbers are right.

signals: History is not mentioned, or "history to be loaded" appears with no years or source.
The plan has no task or time for the history load.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the source owner how far back the source really holds data, and pull one month of the oldest year in scope through the pipeline.

checks.title: Source can bear the history extract
checks.question: Can the source system take the load of the history extract, and is the extract split into chunks that can each be retried?
checks.why: A single five-year query against the source database ran for nine hours, hit an undo limit and failed at ninety percent; it failed again the next night and slowed the source for its users.

evidence.looks_like: An extract split by date or key range, an agreed extract window with the source owner, and an estimate of run time per chunk from a real trial.

signals: The history load is one step with no chunking or restart point.
Source owners are not listed as reviewers of the extract approach.
checks.fail_fast: Time the extract of one realistic chunk against the real source in its normal busy window and multiply out; agree the result with the source owner.

checks.title: Handing over from history load to incremental loads
checks.question: How does the switch from the history or full load to incremental loads avoid both a gap and an overlap in the data?
checks.why: The full snapshot finished at 10:00 but incremental capture was started at 11:00; an hour of changes was never loaded and the totals were quietly short for months.

evidence.looks_like: A defined high-water mark or change position taken before the snapshot starts, incremental capture starting from it, and overlapping rows absorbed by a merge on key.

checks.fail_fast: In test, change rows in the source while the full load runs, then start incremental; every changed row must appear once with its latest value.

checks.title: Reloading or backfilling a past period
checks.question: Can a single past period (a day, a month) be reloaded or backfilled on demand without touching other periods or rebuilding everything?
checks.why: A source bug corrupted three days in March; the only way to fix them was a full rebuild that took the platform down for a weekend.

evidence.looks_like: Pipelines parameterised by period, writes that replace exactly that period, a runbook step for reloading a period, and a note on which downstream tables must also be rebuilt.

signals: The runbook has no reload or backfill procedure.
Jobs read "today" from the clock instead of taking the period as a parameter.
checks.fail_fast: In test, reload one day from three days ago with a parameter and check that only that day's rows and its downstream aggregates changed.

checks.title: Which tables keep history, and for how long
checks.question: For each table, has the business decided whether to keep the history of changes or only the latest value, and for how long?
checks.why: Customer region was stored as latest only; when a sales team was reorganised, last year's sales by region were silently restated and the bonus calculation was disputed.

evidence.looks_like: A list of entities and attributes with "history kept" or "latest only", a retention period, and the business owner who agreed it.

signals: The data model has no statement about history for dimensions.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the main report owner "should last year's figures change when a customer moves region?" and record the answer as a decision.

checks.title: History rows stay correct on reruns and out-of-order changes
checks.question: Does the history logic (effective from and to dates, current flag) stay correct when a load is rerun, when two changes arrive in one batch, or when changes arrive out of order?
checks.why: A rerun closed and reopened every current row, and an older change arriving late became "current", so customers showed last year's address with overlapping validity periods.

evidence.looks_like: Changes ordered by a source sequence or change timestamp, not arrival time; a hash to skip unchanged rows; and tests for rerun, two-changes-per-batch and out-of-order cases.

checks.fail_fast: Feed three versions of one record in reverse order, then rerun the same batch; exactly one current row and no overlapping date ranges may remain.

checks.title: A business key that can change
checks.question: Can a source's business key ever change (renumbering, merges, re-registration), and how is the identity of the thing kept across that change?
checks.why: The source renumbered accounts during a migration; each renumbered account became a new customer, splitting its history and doubling the customer count.

evidence.looks_like: Surrogate keys owned by the platform, a mapping from old to new source keys, and the source owner's confirmation of whether keys can change.

checks.fail_fast: Ask each source owner directly whether keys are ever reused, merged or renumbered, and check a real extract for one key mapping to two names over time.

checks.title: Facts joined to the right version of history
checks.question: When facts are joined to a dimension that keeps history, are they matched to the version valid at the time of the fact, and is that the rule consumers expect?
checks.why: Facts were joined to the current customer row; reports that should show sales by the region at the time showed today's region instead, and nobody had written down which was wanted.

evidence.looks_like: For each report, whether it shows "as it was" or "as it is now", and joins that use the fact date within the validity range or the surrogate key captured at load.

checks.fail_fast: Take one customer who changed region last year and check a sales report shows each sale under the region the business expects.

checks.title: Late and corrected rows rebuild the right periods
checks.question: When rows arrive late or yesterday's figures are corrected next week, which periods are rebuilt, and how far back can corrections reach?
checks.why: Returns were booked against sales from three weeks earlier, but the pipeline only rebuilt the last two days, so monthly net revenue never matched the finance ledger.

evidence.looks_like: A profile of how late data really arrives, an agreed correction window, and a design that reprocesses affected periods by business date rather than load date.

signals: Aggregates are described as built "for the load date" only.
Nothing in the discovery document says how late source data can arrive.
