checks.fail_fast: In a real extract, compare business date against load date and find the longest lag; then insert a row two weeks late in test and check the monthly total updates.

checks.title: Facts arriving before their reference data
checks.question: What happens to a fact row whose customer, product or other reference record has not arrived yet?
checks.why: Orders for new products arrived hours before the product feed; an inner join silently dropped them, and the new-launch report showed zero sales on launch day.

evidence.looks_like: An "unknown" or placeholder member, or a quarantine with automatic reprocessing, and a step that re-points facts once the reference record arrives.

signals: Joins between facts and reference tables are described as inner joins with no handling of misses.
checks.fail_fast: Load a fact row whose reference key does not exist yet, then load the reference row; the fact must be kept and end up attached to the right reference record.

checks.title: Event time, watermarks and late events in streams
checks.question: Do streaming aggregations use event time, how long do they wait for late events (the watermark), and what happens to events later than that?
checks.why: The window waited ten minutes, but mobile clients uploaded events hours later after going offline; those events were silently discarded and daily active users were understated.

evidence.looks_like: The lateness of real events measured, a watermark chosen from that, and a stated home for events beyond it (a correction batch or a side table) agreed with consumers.

checks.fail_fast: Measure the gap between event time and arrival time in a day of real events and see what share falls beyond the proposed watermark.

checks.title: Time zones and business dates
checks.question: Which time zone does each source use, how are timestamps stored, and which time zone defines a business day?
checks.why: One source sent local time and another sent universal time; orders placed late in the evening fell into the next day and daily sales never matched the stores' own reports.

evidence.looks_like: The time zone of every source timestamp, a single storage convention, a defined business-day time zone, and a rule for daylight-saving changes.

signals: The data dictionary lists timestamps without a time zone.
checks.fail_fast: Pick ten real transactions near midnight and check that their business date matches what the source application shows.

checks.title: Alerts reach someone who can act
checks.question: When a job fails, runs late or data looks wrong, who is alerted, through which channel, and within how long?
checks.why: Failure emails went to a shared mailbox nobody read; a load had failed for four days before a user asked why the report had not changed.

evidence.looks_like: Alerts for failure, lateness against the freshness target and data checks, routed to a named team or on-call rota, with an expected response time.

checks.fail_fast: Make a job fail in test and time how long it takes for a person to know.

checks.title: Every run leaves a record
checks.question: Does every run record what it read, what it wrote, row counts, duration and outcome, in a place that can be queried?
checks.why: A user reported a wrong figure from two weeks ago; with no run records nobody could say which load produced it or which input it came from.

evidence.looks_like: A run log or audit table with run id, inputs, outputs, counts, timings and status, kept for a stated period.

checks.fail_fast: Ask which source file produced a given row in yesterday's table, and see how long it takes to answer.

checks.title: Production watched closely after go-live
checks.question: Were the first weeks in production watched closely (hypercare), with defects closed and operations running it alone before sign-off?
checks.why: The team moved to the next project on go-live day; a slow memory leak failed the job at month-end and nobody who understood it was available.

evidence.looks_like: A hypercare period with daily checks, a log of production issues and their fixes, and a handover point when operations run it alone.

checks.fail_fast: Put hypercare dates, people and exit criteria in the plan now.

checks.title: Jobs wait for their data, not the clock
checks.question: Does each job start when its upstream data is complete, rather than at a fixed time that assumes the upstream has finished?
checks.why: The report job ran at 06:00 assuming the load finished at 05:00; one night the load ran late, and the report published half a day's figures to the whole company.

evidence.looks_like: Dependencies declared between jobs or on completion markers, cross-team dependencies named, and what happens when an upstream is late.

signals: The schedule is a list of fixed times with no dependencies.
checks.fail_fast: Delay an upstream job in test and check that the downstream waits instead of running on stale or partial data.

checks.title: Retries for passing failures only
checks.question: Which failures are retried automatically (timeouts, throttling), how many times and with what wait, and which fail straight away (bad data, logic errors)?
checks.why: Every failure was retried five times; a bad-data error retried for three hours, burning compute and delaying the alert until the morning.

evidence.looks_like: A retry policy per job with limits and back-off, failures classified as transient or permanent, and an alert after the last retry.

checks.fail_fast: In test, cause one timeout and one data error; the first should retry and succeed, the second should fail fast and alert.

checks.title: Restart after failing in the middle
checks.question: If a job fails halfway through writing, is the target left untouched or fully consistent, and can the job restart from the failed step without redoing everything?
checks.why: A job failed after updating three of five tables; reports joined new facts to old dimensions, and rerunning from the start re-applied the first three updates.

evidence.looks_like: Atomic writes per table, a defined restart point per step, consumers reading only completed runs, and a failure-injection test.

checks.fail_fast: Kill a job in test while it is writing, then restart it; outputs must match an uninterrupted run.

checks.title: Two runs writing the same table at once
checks.question: What stops two runs of the same job, or two different jobs, writing to the same table at the same time?
checks.why: A manual rerun overlapped the scheduled run; both merged into the same table, one failed on a conflict, and the other left half-updated rows.

evidence.looks_like: One writer per table by design, a limit of one concurrent run per job, and a runbook rule for manual reruns.

checks.fail_fast: Start the same job twice in test and see what happens to the second run and the table.

checks.title: Recovery time and data loss limits
checks.question: How quickly must the service recover after a major failure, how much data may be lost, and has recovery to those limits been tried?
checks.why: A storage account was deleted by mistake; the backups existed but nobody had tried a restore, and it took four days instead of the four hours the business assumed.

evidence.looks_like: An agreed recovery time and acceptable data loss, a backup or replication design that meets them, and the result of a restore test.

checks.fail_fast: Restore one important table from backup into a test environment and time it.

checks.title: Stream restarts from where it stopped
checks.question: When a streaming job stops or is redeployed, does it resume from its saved position without losing or repeating data, and how is that state protected?
checks.why: A redeploy changed the stream's checkpoint location; the job restarted from the earliest available data, reprocessed a week and flooded downstream tables.

evidence.looks_like: Where progress is saved, how it survives redeploys and code changes, the source retention versus the longest expected outage, and a runbook for resetting a stream.

checks.fail_fast: Stop the stream for longer than a typical outage in test, redeploy a changed version, restart, and compare counts with the source.

checks.title: Volumes and growth stated
checks.question: What are the real volumes per source today (rows, size, files per day), and how much are they expected to grow over the next two to three years?
checks.why: The design was sized from a test sample of a million rows; production sent eight hundred million on month-end and the nightly window was blown on the first close.

evidence.looks_like: Measured volumes per source from real data, peak days (month-end, seasonal), and a growth assumption.

signals: Volumes are missing, or given as "large" or "medium" rather than numbers.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each source owner for the row count of their biggest table on their busiest day, and check one against a real extract.

checks.title: Freshness target measured end to end
checks.question: What freshness or latency is promised (for example, ready by 07:00, or within one minute), and has the full path from source to consumer been timed against it?
checks.why: Each step met its own target, but source export, transfer, three layers and the report refresh added up to ninety minutes against a promised thirty.

evidence.looks_like: A freshness target per consumer, a time budget split across every hop, and a measured end to end time from the thin slice or a test run.

checks.fail_fast: Time one record from source change to visible in the report in the thin slice, and compare with the target.

checks.title: Tested at production volume
checks.question: Has the pipeline been run at production volume, including a peak day and the history load, before go-live?
checks.why: Every test ran on a tenth of the data; the first month-end in production ran out of memory in the biggest join and the finance close waited a day.

evidence.looks_like: A performance test at peak production volume with run times, compute size and cost recorded, and the result compared with the freshness target.

signals: The test strategy has no performance or volume test, or uses only small samples.
checks.fail_fast: Run the heaviest transformation on one full peak day of real (or realistically generated) data and time it.

checks.title: Skewed keys and very large joins
checks.question: Are there hot keys (one customer, one default value, nulls) or joins between two very large tables that will make some steps run far slower than the rest?
checks.why: Half of all rows carried a placeholder customer id; in the big join one worker processed that key for an hour while the others sat idle, and the job missed its window.

evidence.looks_like: Key distributions profiled for the large join keys, and a strategy for skewed keys and large joins (filtering defaults, splitting hot keys, pre-aggregating).

checks.fail_fast: Count rows per join key for the two largest joins and look at the top ten keys' share.

checks.title: Storage layout and file sizes kept healthy
checks.question: How are table layout (partitioning or clustering) and file sizes chosen and maintained, so frequent small writes do not slow reads over time?
checks.why: A streaming load wrote thousands of tiny files an hour; reads slowed every week until a simple query took ten minutes and cost ten times more.

evidence.looks_like: Layout chosen from the main filter and join columns, a scheduled compaction and cleanup job, and a metric for average file size.

checks.fail_fast: After a week of test loads, count files and average file size for the busiest table.

checks.title: Counts and totals reconciled layer by layer
checks.question: Are row counts and key totals compared automatically between the source and each layer on every load, with the differences explained?
checks.why: The report was four percent short of the source and nobody could say in which layer rows had been lost, so a week went into tracing one join that dropped orphan rows.

evidence.looks_like: Counts and sums of key measures captured at the source and after each layer for every run, stored, compared, and every expected difference (filters, quarantined rows) accounted for.

signals: Reconciliation appears only as a one-off test activity, not as part of every run.
checks.fail_fast: For one day of real data, write down the source count and total, then the count and total in each layer, and explain every difference.

checks.title: Matched against a number the business already trusts
checks.question: Are the final numbers checked against an independent figure the business already trusts (a finance ledger, an existing report, a source application screen)?
checks.why: Source-to-target counts all matched, yet the new revenue figure disagreed with the finance ledger because the definition of revenue differed; it was found only at user acceptance.

evidence.looks_like: A named trusted figure for each key measure, the comparison method, and an agreed explanation of known differences.

checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner which existing number they would compare against, and compare one month of thin-slice output with it now.

checks.title: Tolerances and who signs off differences
checks.question: What size of difference is acceptable for each measure, and who decides when a difference is explained well enough to go live?
checks.why: Test found a 0.3 percent gap; engineering called it rounding, finance called it a blocker, and go-live slipped two weeks while they argued.

evidence.looks_like: A tolerance per measure and a named person who accepts reconciliation results.

checks.fail_fast: Put the tolerance question on the next sign-off agenda and record a number for the top three measures.

checks.title: First production loads reconciled
checks.question: Were the first production loads, including the history load, reconciled against the source and trusted figures before users were told to rely on them?
checks.why: Production used a different source instance with extra test records; nobody reconciled the first loads, and dummy orders appeared in the board pack.

evidence.looks_like: A reconciliation result for each of the first production runs, with sign-off, recorded in the hypercare or go-live report.

checks.fail_fast: Add "reconcile first production load" as a go-live checklist item with an owner and a tolerance.

checks.title: Everything that runs is in version control
checks.question: Is everything that runs in production (pipeline code, SQL, job definitions, schedules, data quality rules, permissions) kept in version control?
checks.why: The schedule and parameters were edited by hand in the production interface; when the job was recreated after an incident, nobody knew the real settings and it ran with wrong ones for a week.

evidence.looks_like: A repository layout that includes code, job and schedule definitions and configuration, and a rule that production is never changed by hand.

signals: Jobs are described as "configured in the user interface".
checks.fail_fast: Pick one production job and try to recreate it in a fresh environment only from the repository.

checks.title: Branching and code review
checks.question: What is the branching approach, and must every change be reviewed by another person and pass automated checks before it merges?
checks.why: A developer pushed a join change straight to the main branch on a Friday; it removed a filter, and the weekend loads double-counted refunds.

evidence.looks_like: A short branching model, protected main branch, required reviewer, and automated tests and linting run on every pull request.

checks.fail_fast: Try to push directly to the main branch; it should be refused.

checks.title: Automated promotion of the same build
checks.question: Is the same tested build promoted automatically from development to test to production, with an approval step before production?
checks.why: Each environment was deployed by copying scripts by hand; production ended up with an older version of one script, and test results said nothing about what really ran.

evidence.looks_like: A pipeline that builds once, deploys the same version to each environment with environment settings injected, and records which version is where.

checks.fail_fast: Deploy the thin slice to test using only the pipeline, with nobody clicking in the target environment.

checks.title: Configuration per environment, not in code
checks.question: Are environment-specific values (paths, connection names, schedules, compute sizes) kept in configuration per environment rather than written into the code?
checks.why: A storage path to production was hard-coded in a shared module; tests in development read and then overwrote production data.

evidence.looks_like: A configuration file or variable set per environment, and code that reads all environment values from it.

checks.fail_fast: Search the code for production host names, paths and catalog names; each hit is a defect.

checks.title: No secrets in the repository
checks.question: Are passwords, keys and tokens kept in a secret store and read at run time, never in code, configuration files or the repository's history?
checks.why: A database password was committed in a script; the repository was later shared with a vendor, and the security team had to rotate credentials across four systems.

evidence.looks_like: A named secret store per environment, code that reads secrets by name, and an automated secret scan on the repository.

checks.fail_fast: Run a secret scanner over the whole repository history today.

checks.title: Infrastructure defined as code
checks.question: Are the platform's environments, storage, compute policies, identities and permissions created from code, so another environment can be built identically?
checks.why: The test environment was built by hand months after production and differed in network and permission settings, so tests passed that failed in production.

evidence.looks_like: Infrastructure code in version control covering workspaces, storage, networks, identities, policies and grants, applied through a pipeline.

checks.fail_fast: Build a throwaway environment from the infrastructure code alone and compare its settings with test.

checks.title: Rolling back a release, including its data
checks.question: If a release goes wrong, how are both the code and any data or table structure it changed put back, and has that been rehearsed?
checks.why: A release changed a table's structure and backfilled it; the code could be rolled back in minutes, but the data could not, and reports were broken for two days.

evidence.looks_like: A rollback plan per release covering code, schema and data (restore points or table versions), and a rehearsal in a production-like environment.

signals: The cut-over plan has no rollback section, or says "roll back the code" only.
checks.fail_fast: Deploy a release that changes a table in test, then roll it back fully, and time it.

checks.title: A new column appears at the source
checks.question: When a source adds a column, does the pipeline fail, drop it silently, or carry it through, and is that the agreed behaviour per layer?
checks.why: The source added a discount column; the raw layer dropped it silently, and when finance asked for it three months later the history could not be recovered.

evidence.looks_like: A schema policy per layer (for example: raw keeps everything including unknown columns, cleaned layers change only through a reviewed change), and an alert when a new column appears.

signals: The architecture does not mention schema changes at all.
checks.fail_fast: Add a column to a test source file or table and run the pipeline; see what each layer does and whether anyone is told.

checks.title: A column renamed, removed or retyped
checks.question: When a source renames, removes or changes the type of a column, does the pipeline stop loudly before writing wrong data?
checks.why: A source changed an amount column from cents to a decimal in dollars; the pipeline cast it happily and revenue fell a hundredfold in the morning report.

evidence.looks_like: An expected schema checked on every load, breaking changes failing the load with a clear alert, and range or distribution checks on key measures.

checks.fail_fast: In test, rename one column and change one type in a source sample; the load must fail with a message that names the column.

checks.title: Source owners warn before they change
checks.question: Is there an agreement (a data contract or a change notice) that source owners tell the data team before changing structure or meaning?
checks.why: The source team released a new version on a Friday with restructured tables; nobody told the data team and the weekend loads failed, missing a regulatory deadline.

evidence.looks_like: A written agreement or contract per source naming the schema, the notice period for changes, and a contact; source release calendars known to the team.

signals: Source owners are not in the stakeholder map.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each source owner when their next release is and whether it changes anything the project reads.

checks.title: Personal and sensitive data found and classified
checks.question: Which columns hold personal or sensitive data, in which sources and layers, and is each classified?
checks.why: Free-text notes held customer phone numbers and health details; nobody had classified them, so they were copied unmasked into a table hundreds of analysts could read.

evidence.looks_like: A classification for every column in scope (public, internal, confidential, personal, special category), including free-text fields, recorded in the data dictionary or catalog.

signals: Personal data is not mentioned, or mentioned only as "will follow policy".
checks.fail_fast: Scan a real extract of each source for patterns like emails, phone numbers and national ids, including in free-text columns.

checks.title: Who can see what
checks.question: Who may see which tables, rows and columns, and how is that enforced (masking, row filters, separate views) rather than trusted?
checks.why: Regional managers were meant to see only their own region, but the report filtered it in the front end; anyone querying the table directly saw every region's salaries.

evidence.looks_like: An access matrix by group, enforced in the data platform itself with masking and row-level rules, and tests that run as each persona.

checks.fail_fast: Log in as a test user of the lowest-privilege persona and query the most sensitive table directly.

checks.title: Retention and the right to be forgotten
checks.question: How long is each kind of data kept, and how is a person's data erased everywhere it lives, including history tables, old table versions, backups and extracts?
checks.why: A customer's erasure request deleted their current row, but the history table, old file versions kept for recovery and a weekly extract to a partner still held their data.

evidence.looks_like: A retention period per data class, an erasure procedure that covers every layer, history, versions and copies, and the time it takes to complete.

checks.fail_fast: Trace one test person through every table, version and extract in test and count where their data would remain after the erasure procedure.

checks.title: Access is audited
checks.question: Is every read and change of sensitive data logged with who, what and when, and does someone review it?
checks.why: After a data leak, the team could not say who had queried the customer table in the last month, and the regulator treated the whole table as exposed.

evidence.looks_like: Audit logs switched on for data access, kept for the regulated period, and a named reviewer with a review frequency.

checks.fail_fast: Query a sensitive test table, then find that query in the audit log within an hour.

checks.title: Regulations and where data may live
checks.question: Which regulations apply to the data (privacy, industry, residency), and does the design keep data, copies and processing in permitted locations?
checks.why: A disaster-recovery copy was configured to another region outside the permitted jurisdiction; the audit found it a week before go-live and the platform design had to change.

evidence.looks_like: A list of applicable regulations, permitted regions for storage, processing and backups, and sign-off from the data protection or compliance owner.

checks.fail_fast: Ask the compliance owner which locations are permitted, and list every place the design puts a copy of the data.

checks.title: A contract with each consumer
checks.question: For each consumer (report, extract, application, model), is there an agreed contract: the tables or fields they use, their meaning, grain, freshness and how they will receive it?
checks.why: A downstream team built a pricing model on an internal staging table; a routine refactor renamed it and the pricing model failed on a sale day.

evidence.looks_like: A list of consumers and, for each, the published interface, its fields and meaning, grain, freshness promise and a named contact.

signals: Consumers are listed by name only, with no interface or freshness.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the main consumer which exact fields they will read; check each is in the data model with a definition.

checks.title: Consumers can tell whether data is complete
checks.question: Can a consumer see when the data was last refreshed and whether today's load is complete, before they rely on it?
checks.why: The load failed overnight but the dashboard looked normal; the sales director presented yesterday's numbers as today's to the board.

evidence.looks_like: A visible "data as of" time on reports, a completeness flag or status table, and a way to warn consumers when a load is late.

checks.fail_fast: Stop the load in test and look at the report as a user would; can you tell it is stale?

checks.title: Changes to what consumers use are announced
checks.question: How are breaking changes to published tables or interfaces versioned and announced, so consumers have time to adapt?
checks.why: A column was renamed for consistency in a minor release; three reports and a partner extract broke the next morning.

evidence.looks_like: A rule separating published interfaces from internal tables, a versioning or deprecation approach with a notice period, and a list of who to tell.

checks.fail_fast: Find out how the team would learn which consumers use a given column today.

checks.title: Business definitions live in one place
checks.question: Is each business measure (revenue, active customer) defined and calculated once, in a shared model, rather than separately in each report?
checks.why: Three dashboards calculated margin three ways; the leadership meeting spent an hour arguing about which number was right instead of deciding anything.

evidence.looks_like: A definitions list with the owner of each measure, implemented once in a shared model or semantic layer that reports reuse.

checks.fail_fast: Ask two consumers to write down how they calculate the top measure; compare the answers.

checks.title: Consumer queries fast enough under real load
checks.question: Will reports, interfaces and extracts respond fast enough when the expected number of users or calls hit them at the same time?
checks.why: The dashboard was quick in testing with one user; on Monday morning two hundred managers opened it at once and it took two minutes per page.

evidence.looks_like: Expected concurrent users or calls and response targets, the serving design (aggregates, caching, sizing), and a concurrency test result.

checks.fail_fast: Run the slowest report query twenty times at once against realistic data and time it.

checks.title: Test levels that include data tests
checks.question: Does the test strategy cover code tests, data tests (rules, reconciliation), integration end to end, performance and user acceptance, each with an owner?
checks.why: Tests checked that each function worked on hand-made rows; nobody tested the real data end to end, and the first integrated run produced reports nobody recognised.

evidence.looks_like: A test strategy naming each test level, what it proves, who runs it, where, and with what data, including data quality and reconciliation tests.

signals: The test strategy says "to be defined", or covers only unit tests and user acceptance.
checks.fail_fast: For each top requirement, write the one data test that would prove it, and see which ones you cannot write.

checks.title: Realistic, safe test data
checks.question: Where does test data come from, is it realistic enough to find real problems (volumes, edge cases, bad rows), and is personal data masked or synthetic?
checks.why: Test data was a tidy hand-made sample with no nulls or duplicates; every test passed, and the first real load failed on problems the sample could never have shown.

evidence.looks_like: A source of test data per environment (masked copy, sampled production, generated), the edge cases it includes, and security approval.

checks.fail_fast: Compare the null, duplicate and orphan-key rates of the test data with the real-data profile.

checks.title: Automated tests run on every change
checks.question: Do automated tests (code and data) run on every change in the release pipeline, and does a failure stop the release?
checks.why: A small refactor changed a join; the tests existed but were run by hand and nobody ran them, so the regression reached production.

evidence.looks_like: Tests wired into the pull request and deployment pipeline as required gates, with coverage of the transformations that carry business rules.

checks.fail_fast: Break one business rule deliberately on a branch; the pipeline must fail before merge.

checks.title: Users test with numbers they recognise
checks.question: Will business users accept the solution by checking real numbers they know, against agreed criteria, rather than by looking at screens?
checks.why: User acceptance was a demo of the dashboard layout; the first time finance compared it with their own numbers was after go-live, and they rejected it.

evidence.looks_like: User acceptance scenarios with expected figures supplied by the business, named testers, dates, and sign-off criteria.

checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner for three numbers they know by heart and check them in the thin slice.

checks.title: Failure, rerun and recovery tested on purpose
checks.question: Does the test plan include deliberate failures: reruns, duplicate input, late data, schema changes, empty input and jobs killed mid-run?
checks.why: Every test assumed the happy path; in the first month the pipeline met a resent file, a late batch and a crash mid-write, and each one corrupted data.

evidence.looks_like: Negative test cases for each failure the design claims to handle, with expected outcomes.

checks.fail_fast: List every failure the architecture says it handles and check each has a test case.

databricks.name: Databricks
databricks.version_note: Checked against docs.databricks.com on 2026-11-01. Product names used here: Unity Catalog, Lakeflow Jobs, Lakeflow pipelines (formerly Delta Live Tables / DLT), AUTO CDC (formerly APPLY CHANGES), Declarative Automation Bundles (formerly Databricks Asset Bundles), data quality monitoring (formerly anomaly detection) and data profiling (formerly Lakehouse Monitoring). Names move fast; re-check before quoting them to a client.

DUP-01.do: Ingest files with Auto Loader or COPY INTO, which both remember files already loaded. Write to silver with MERGE on the business key, not append.
DUP-01.verify: Re-drop the same file and rerun; DESCRIBE HISTORY on the target shows no rows inserted (operationMetrics numTargetRowsInserted = 0).
DUP-01.traps: A file renamed or rewritten by the source counts as new to Auto Loader. Its checkpoint is the memory: deleting or moving it reloads everything.

DUP-02.do: Use MERGE on a key, or INSERT OVERWRITE / replaceWhere for a whole date range, for every write a rerun could repeat.
DUP-02.verify: Run the job twice for the same period; compare counts and DESCRIBE HISTORY metrics between runs.
DUP-02.traps: Repairing a failed Lakeflow Jobs run reruns failed tasks from the start; a task that appended before failing will append again.

DUP-03.do: Profile key uniqueness with a GROUP BY key HAVING count(*) > 1 query; deduplicate in silver with a window (row_number over key ordered by a change timestamp) before MERGE.
DUP-03.verify: A uniqueness expectation or test on the silver key runs on every load.
DUP-03.traps: MERGE fails when several source rows match one target row; deduplicate the source batch first. PRIMARY KEY constraints in Unity Catalog are informational and are not enforced.

DUP-04.do: In Structured Streaming use dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark on an event id, and idempotent writes in foreachBatch (MERGE, or txnAppId plus txnVersion options).
DUP-04.verify: Restart a stream from an older checkpoint copy in test and compare counts.
DUP-04.traps: dropDuplicates without a watermark keeps state forever and grows until the job slows or fails.

HIST-01.do: Load history into the same bronze tables as daily loads, by date chunk, from archive files or a source extract; record the chunks in a control table.
HIST-01.verify: Reconcile each historical year against the source or finance before switching on daily loads.

HIST-02.do: For JDBC reads, set partitionColumn, lowerBound, upperBound and numPartitions and keep parallel connections within what the source owner agreed; or land extracts as files instead.
HIST-02.verify: Time one chunk against the source in its busy window.
HIST-02.traps: Too many partitions in a JDBC read opens that many connections at once against the source.

HIST-03.do: With Lakeflow pipelines, AUTO CDC with SEQUENCE BY absorbs overlap between the snapshot and the change feed; otherwise MERGE with a sequence column so older changes never overwrite newer.
HIST-03.verify: Change rows during the snapshot in test and check each ends with its latest value once.

HIST-04.do: Pass the period as a job parameter and write with replaceWhere on the date column; keep a separate backfill job or bundle target for large reloads.
HIST-04.verify: Reload one past day in test; DESCRIBE HISTORY shows only that day's files were rewritten.
HIST-04.traps: A full refresh of a Lakeflow pipeline streaming table re-reads all source data and clears the table first; check source retention before pressing it.

LATE-01.do: Rebuild aggregates for affected business dates with MERGE or replaceWhere driven by the dates present in the incoming batch; Change Data Feed on silver can tell gold which keys changed.
LATE-01.verify: Insert a row with an old business date in test and check the gold total for that date changes.

LATE-02.do: Insert an unknown-member row in each dimension and left join facts to it; or quarantine misses to a table and reprocess it in a scheduled task.
LATE-02.verify: An expectation or test counts facts pointing at the unknown member over time.

LATE-03.do: Set withWatermark on the event-time column from measured lateness; route later events to a side table.
LATE-03.verify: Check the streaming query progress metrics for numRowsDroppedByWatermark.
LATE-03.traps: A watermark that is too long holds more state and costs memory; too short silently drops events.

LATE-04.do: Store timestamps as TIMESTAMP (universal time) and convert with from_utc_timestamp for the business-day time zone; set the session time zone deliberately rather than relying on defaults.
LATE-04.verify: Compare business dates of near-midnight rows with the source application.
LATE-04.traps: TIMESTAMP_NTZ has no time zone; mixing it with TIMESTAMP across sources shifts hours.

DEL-01.do: With CDC feeds use AUTO CDC ... APPLY AS DELETE WHEN, or MERGE ... WHEN MATCHED AND op = 'D' THEN DELETE; without CDC, compare full key snapshots (AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT treats missing keys as deleted) or use MERGE ... WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE.
DEL-01.verify: Delete a row in a source test system and check it disappears or is flagged after the load.
DEL-01.traps: WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE against a partial extract deletes everything not in that extract.

DEL-03.do: Enable Change Data Feed on silver so downstream jobs see deletes and rebuild affected aggregates.
DEL-03.verify: After a test delete, gold totals equal the sum of silver detail.

SCD-02.do: Prefer AUTO CDC ... STORED AS SCD TYPE 2 with SEQUENCE BY on a source sequence; it places out-of-order changes in the right history position. Hand-written MERGE needs a hash of tracked columns and ordering by sequence.
SCD-02.verify: Feed reversed versions and a rerun in test; check no overlapping __START_AT / __END_AT ranges.
SCD-02.traps: Sequencing by ingestion time instead of a source sequence breaks history when changes arrive out of order.

SCD-03.do: Generate surrogate keys with an IDENTITY column on the dimension; keep a source-key mapping table.
SCD-03.traps: IDENTITY values are unique but not consecutive, and declaring one limits concurrent writes to the table.

SCH-01.do: Choose an Auto Loader schemaEvolutionMode per source: addNewColumns (default when no schema is given; stream stops once, then continues with the new column), rescue (new columns go to _rescued_data), failOnNewColumns, or none. In silver, use MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION only where agreed.
SCH-01.verify: Drop a test file with an extra column and watch what the stream and the target do.
SCH-01.traps: With addNewColumns the stream fails on purpose and must be restarted; make sure the job has retries, or it stays down overnight.

SCH-02.do: Supply an explicit schema or schema hints for critical columns; let Delta schema enforcement reject mismatched writes; add CHECK constraints for ranges.
SCH-02.verify: A test file with a renamed or retyped column fails the load with a clear error.
SCH-02.traps: Type mismatches can land in _rescued_data quietly; alert when that column is not null.

DQ-01.do: In Lakeflow pipelines write rules as expectations (EXPECT ... ON VIOLATION DROP ROW / FAIL UPDATE); elsewhere use CHECK and NOT NULL constraints plus a test framework in jobs.
DQ-01.verify: Query the pipeline event log or Data quality tab for pass and fail counts per rule.

DQ-02.do: Use warn or drop expectations, and write failing rows to a quarantine table with an inverted expectation so they are kept with a reason, not just counted.
DQ-02.verify: Load known-bad rows in test and find each one in quarantine.
DQ-02.traps: expect_or_drop only counts dropped rows; the rows themselves are gone unless you quarantine them.

DQ-03.do: Read files with a rescued data column (Auto Loader) or badRecordsPath, so malformed records are kept aside instead of failing the stream.
DQ-03.verify: Put a malformed record in a test file; the rest loads and the bad record is readable.

DQ-04.do: Enable data quality monitoring on the schema for freshness and completeness, and add a row-count check task that fails on empty or abnormal batches; alert with Databricks SQL alerts.
DQ-04.verify: Load an empty file in test and confirm an alert fires.
DQ-04.traps: Monitoring results arrive after the load; a gate inside the job is still needed to stop bad data reaching gold.

DQ-05.do: Profile real extracts with SQL in a notebook or with data profiling on the bronze tables.

REC-01.do: Write per-run counts and sums per layer to a reconciliation table from each task; DESCRIBE HISTORY operationMetrics give rows written per commit.
REC-01.verify: A dashboard or query compares source and each layer per run.

PERF-03.do: Run on a production-sized copy (a deep clone in a test catalog, or generated data) on the production compute configuration; read the Spark UI or query profile for spill and skew.
PERF-03.verify: Record run time, compute size and cost from system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline and system.billing.usage.

PERF-04.do: Rely on adaptive query execution for skewed joins, broadcast small tables, filter null and placeholder keys before joins, and salt only when AQE is not enough.
PERF-04.verify: In the Spark UI, compare the longest task against the median for the big join stage.

PERF-05.do: Use liquid clustering on the main filter or merge columns for new tables; let predictive optimization run OPTIMIZE and VACUUM on Unity Catalog managed tables.
PERF-05.verify: DESCRIBE DETAIL shows numFiles and sizeInBytes; DESCRIBE HISTORY shows OPTIMIZE runs.
PERF-05.traps: Predictive optimization covers managed tables only; external tables need scheduled OPTIMIZE and VACUUM. Check that clustering keys match the MERGE condition, or merges scan the whole table.

COST-01.do: Read the thin slice's cost from system.billing.usage joined to system.billing.list_prices, by job.
COST-01.verify: Compare the estimate with the first month of production usage from the same tables.
COST-01.traps: List price is not your contract price; agree discounts with whoever holds the contract.

COST-02.do: Use compute policies to cap node types and worker counts and to force auto-termination and tags; set account budgets with alerts per workspace or tag.
COST-02.verify: Try to create oversized compute as a developer in development; the policy should block it.
COST-02.traps: Budgets alert, they do not cap general spend; serverless usage policies only tag usage for attribution. Real limits come from policies and permissions.

COST-03.do: Enforce custom tags through compute policies for classic compute and serverless usage policies for serverless; report from system.billing.usage custom_tags.
COST-03.verify: Query the share of last week's usage with no project tag.

COST-04.do: Use job compute or serverless for scheduled work instead of all-purpose clusters; set auto-termination; wait for upstream data with file-arrival or table-update triggers, not sleeping tasks.
COST-04.verify: Compare job duration with compute uptime in system tables for the top jobs.
COST-04.traps: A continuous Lakeflow pipeline or stream runs compute all day; use triggered mode when freshness allows.

SEC-01.do: Apply governed tags for classification on columns in Unity Catalog; data classification can suggest tags.
SEC-01.verify: Query information_schema column tags to list sensitive columns and their owners.

SEC-02.do: Grant to groups in Unity Catalog; apply row filters and column masks, or ABAC policies on governed tags at catalog or schema level for many tables.
SEC-02.verify: Query the table as a test user from the lowest persona.
SEC-02.traps: Row filters and masks need recent runtimes (older compute returns no data), cannot be put on views, and block time travel and clones on that table.

SEC-03.do: DELETE the person's rows in every layer, then VACUUM so old files are removed; deletion vectors need a REORG ... APPLY (PURGE) before VACUUM to physically remove rows.
SEC-03.verify: After the procedure, time travel to an earlier version and confirm the data is gone once retention has passed.
SEC-03.traps: Time travel, deep clones and exports keep copies until each is cleaned too.

SEC-04.do: Query system.access.audit for data access events; keep it for the regulated period.
SEC-04.verify: Find a test query against a sensitive table in system.access.audit.

ENV-01.do: Separate workspaces or at least separate catalogs per environment, bound to their workspaces with workspace-catalog binding, and separate storage locations.
ENV-01.verify: A development service principal cannot write to the production catalog.

ENV-02.do: Grant privileges to account groups, make groups (not people) owners of catalogs, schemas and jobs, and run jobs as service principals.
ENV-02.verify: Check job run_as and object owners; none should be a named person in production.

ENV-03.do: For private sources, plan private connectivity (for serverless, network connectivity configurations) and Unity Catalog connections or credentials early.
ENV-03.traps: Serverless and classic compute reach the network differently; prove the route for the compute you will really use.

REL-01.do: Keep code in Git folders and jobs, pipelines and schedules as bundle resources in the repository.
REL-01.verify: Recreate a job from the repository into an empty workspace with a bundle deploy.
REL-01.traps: Jobs edited in the UI drift from the bundle; restrict edit rights in production.

REL-03.do: Use Declarative Automation Bundles with one target per environment; CI runs databricks bundle validate and deploy with a service principal.
REL-03.verify: The production deployment history shows only the CI service principal deploying.

REL-04.do: Use bundle variables and target overrides for catalog names, paths and compute sizes.
REL-04.verify: Search the code for production catalog names outside the bundle configuration.

REL-05.do: Keep secrets in secret scopes (optionally backed by the cloud key store) and read them with dbutils.secrets; prefer Unity Catalog connections and service credentials over passwords in code.
REL-05.traps: Secrets printed in a notebook cell are redacted, but derived strings and logs can still leak them.

REL-06.do: Define workspaces, catalogs, grants, policies and storage credentials with the Databricks Terraform provider; bundles for jobs and pipelines.

REL-07.do: Use RESTORE TABLE ... TO VERSION AS OF for data rollback, within the retention window; redeploy the previous bundle version for code.
REL-07.verify: Rehearse RESTORE on a test table after a schema-changing release.
REL-07.traps: RESTORE only works for versions VACUUM has not cleaned up.

ORCH-01.do: Use task dependencies inside a job, and table-update or file-arrival triggers across jobs.
ORCH-01.verify: Delay an upstream table in test and check the downstream job does not start.

ORCH-02.do: Set task retries and minimum retry interval, plus job and task timeouts and duration warnings.
ORCH-02.traps: Retrying a non-idempotent task duplicates data; fix idempotency before adding retries.

ORCH-03.do: Each Delta write is atomic per table; split multi-table updates into tasks and use repair runs to rerun only failed tasks and those after them.
ORCH-03.verify: Cancel a run mid-task in test, repair it, and compare outputs with a clean run.
ORCH-03.traps: A repair reruns the whole failed task from the beginning, not from the failed row.

ORCH-04.do: Keep maximum concurrent runs at 1 (the default for new jobs) and use queueing for triggered jobs.
ORCH-04.traps: Two different jobs writing one table can still conflict; Delta raises concurrent modification errors on overlapping files.

ORCH-05.do: Decide which tables need deep clones or storage replication to another region; time travel is not a backup, because VACUUM removes old files.
ORCH-05.verify: Restore a table from the chosen backup into a test catalog and time it.

ORCH-06.do: Give every stream a fixed, environment-specific checkpoint location and keep it with the table; in Lakeflow pipelines checkpoints are managed for you.
ORCH-06.verify: Redeploy a changed stream in test and confirm it resumes from its position.
ORCH-06.traps: Some query changes are not allowed with an existing checkpoint (for example changes to stateful operations); plan a reset and backfill when they are needed.

OPS-01.do: Configure job notifications to a team channel or paging tool, plus duration-warning notifications for lateness.
OPS-01.verify: Fail a test job and time the alert.

OPS-03.do: Use system.lakeflow job and task run tables and DESCRIBE HISTORY for run records; add an audit table for business counts.
OPS-03.verify: Trace a row in gold to its job run and source file (_metadata.file_path captured in bronze).

TEST-02.do: Use shallow or deep clones of masked production tables into a test catalog, or generated data.
TEST-02.traps: Clones of tables with row filters or masks are not supported; mask before cloning.

TEST-03.do: Run unit tests with pytest locally or with Databricks Connect, and data tests in a CI job deployed by the bundle to a test target.

SERV-02.do: Publish a status table or use table health in Catalog Explorer from data quality monitoring; show last refresh time on AI/BI dashboards.

SERV-04.do: Define shared measures once as Unity Catalog metric views and point dashboards and Genie spaces at them.
SERV-04.traps: Metric views are newer; check the feature's status in your workspace before standardising on it.

SERV-05.do: Serve reports from a SQL warehouse sized and scaled for concurrency; pre-aggregate heavy gold tables or use materialized views.
SERV-05.verify: Run concurrent queries and read the warehouse's query history for queueing time.

checks.title: Unity Catalog objects owned by groups
checks.question: Are catalogs, schemas, tables, jobs and pipelines owned by groups or service principals, with privileges granted to account groups rather than individual users?
checks.why: A catalog owned by a contractor's user account could not be changed after the contractor left, until an admin reassigned ownership in the middle of an incident.

evidence.looks_like: An ownership and grant model by group per catalog and schema, defined in code.

checks.fail_fast: List owners of production catalogs, schemas and jobs from information_schema and the jobs list; flag every individual user.

checks.title: Compute policies cap size and force shutdown
checks.question: Do compute policies limit node types and worker counts, force auto-termination and required tags, and are users unable to create compute without a policy?
checks.why: Without policies a developer created a large all-purpose cluster with no auto-termination, and it ran idle for two weeks.

evidence.looks_like: Named policies per workload type, who may use each, and unrestricted cluster creation removed.

checks.fail_fast: As a normal user, try to create compute without a policy and above the policy's size.

checks.title: Serverless usage tagged for attribution
checks.question: Is serverless compute (notebooks, jobs, pipelines) attributed to projects through serverless usage policies, and is the team aware these tag usage rather than cap it?
checks.why: Serverless spend grew quickly across teams with no tags, so it showed as one untraceable line on the bill.

evidence.looks_like: Serverless usage policies per project or team, assigned to the right groups, and a cost report by their tags.

checks.fail_fast: Query system.billing.usage for serverless usage in the last week with no project tag.

checks.title: Table retention matches time travel and recovery needs
checks.question: Is delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration (and log retention) set per table to match how far back the team needs time travel, RESTORE and stream recovery, balanced against storage cost and erasure rules?
checks.why: A bad release was found eight days later; VACUUM had already removed files older than the default seven days, so RESTORE to the good version was impossible.

evidence.looks_like: A retention setting per table class, justified by recovery needs and personal-data erasure deadlines.

checks.fail_fast: Run SHOW TBLPROPERTIES on key tables and compare retention with how long defects usually take to find.

checks.title: Auto Loader schema evolution mode chosen per source
checks.question: For each Auto Loader source, is the schema evolution mode (addNewColumns, rescue, failOnNewColumns, none) chosen deliberately, with the job set to restart after an intentional stop?
checks.why: With the default addNewColumns mode, a new source column stopped the stream as designed, but the job had no retries and the stream stayed down all night.

evidence.looks_like: The mode per source, where rescued data is monitored, and retries on the ingestion task.

checks.fail_fast: Drop a file with a new column in test and see whether the job recovers without a person.

checks.title: Job retries, concurrency and repair are safe
checks.question: Are task retries, timeouts, maximum concurrent runs and queueing set deliberately for each job, and is every task safe to rerun from the start, as a repair run does?
checks.why: Operations repaired a failed run; the failed task had appended half its rows before failing, and the repair appended them again.

evidence.looks_like: Retry and timeout settings per task in the bundle, concurrency left at one, and a runbook note on repair.

checks.fail_fast: Cancel a task halfway in test, repair the run, and compare the output with a clean run.

checks.title: Pipeline expectations with the right action
checks.question: In Lakeflow pipelines, does each expectation use the right action (warn, drop row, fail update), and are dropped rows kept somewhere for reprocessing?
checks.why: Every rule was set to drop; thousands of rows a day were silently removed and only a count was logged.

evidence.looks_like: A rule list mapping each expectation to an action, plus a quarantine table for dropped rows.

checks.fail_fast: Count expectations by action in the pipeline code and check each drop has a quarantine.

checks.title: Promotion through bundles, run as service principals
checks.question: Are jobs, pipelines and dashboards deployed to each environment through Declarative Automation Bundles (formerly Asset Bundles) from CI, with production jobs running as a service principal?
checks.why: Production jobs were created by hand in the UI and ran as the developer; a later bundle deploy created duplicates and both copies wrote to the same tables.

evidence.looks_like: A bundle with dev, test and prod targets, run_as a service principal in prod, deployed only by CI.

checks.fail_fast: Deploy the thin slice to the test target with databricks bundle deploy from a CI pipeline.

checks.title: System tables used for cost and run monitoring
checks.question: Are system tables (billing usage and prices, job run timeline, audit, query history) available to the people who need them, with a cost and reliability view built on them?
checks.why: Nobody had been granted access to the system catalog, so a cost spike was investigated for a week from the invoice instead of in an hour from the usage table.

evidence.looks_like: Grants on the system catalog to platform and finance groups, and a dashboard by job, tag and day.

checks.fail_fast: Query yesterday's cost by job from system.billing.usage and list prices.

checks.title: Managed or external tables decided
checks.question: Is the choice between Unity Catalog managed and external tables, and the storage location for each catalog, decided and recorded?
checks.why: Tables were created as external by habit; predictive optimization did not run on them, small files built up, and dropping a table left its data behind in storage.

evidence.looks_like: A decision record on table types and managed storage locations per catalog.

checks.fail_fast: Count production tables by table type in information_schema.tables.

checks.title: AUTO CDC sequenced by a real source order
checks.question: Where AUTO CDC builds SCD tables, is SEQUENCE BY a column that truly reflects source change order (with a tie-breaker), not the time the row landed?
checks.why: Sequencing used the file arrival time; a delayed file replayed older updates as newest, and SCD type 2 history showed customers moving back to old addresses.

evidence.looks_like: The sequence column per source, how ties are broken (STRUCT of columns), and the delete condition.

checks.fail_fast: Ask the source owner which column orders changes, and check for ties in a real change extract.
